claims.source: Uncoupler proteins merely serve an auxiliary function under cold stress, as shown by the fact that, in mice, ablation of the major uncoupling protein UCP1 is nonlethal (Enerbäck et al., 1997) and does not affect basal body temperature.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by citation to Enerbäck et al., 1997.

claims.claim: Using MTY, intramitochondrial temperature in respiring human HEK293-derived cells is at least 10–12°C higher than the ambient temperature at which the cells are maintained.
claims.source: Using the mitochondrially targeted fluorescent dye Mito Thermo Yellow (MTY), it was recently shown that intramitochondrial temperature in respiring, human HEK293-derived (immortalised embryonic kidney) cells is at least 10–12°C higher than the ambient temperature at which the cells are maintained (Chrétien et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chrétien et al., 2018, a previous study by the authors.

claims.claim: MTY fluorescence change after cells were treated with OXPHOS inhibitors indicated a temperature drop of 10-12°C magnitude, based on internal calibration.
claims.source: In essence, this inference was based on the fact that the MTY fluorescence change, after cells were treated with OXPHOS inhibitors such as rotenone (targeted on OXPHOS complex I, cI), antimycin (targeted on OXPHOS complex III, cIII), or oligomycin (targeted on ATP synthase – OXPHOS complex V, cV), or subjected to prolonged anaerobiosis, indicated a temperature drop of this magnitude, based on internal calibration at the end of each experiment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chrétien et al., 2018, describing the methodology and findings of the previous study.

claims.claim: Inferences from the use of protein-based fluorescence probes targeted to mitochondria are similar to those from MTY.
claims.source: Inferences from the use of protein-based fluorescence probes targeted to mitochondria are similar (Nakano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nakano et al., 2017, which used protein-based temperature probes.

claims.claim: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is at a temperature distinct from the extracellular environment.
claims.source: In addition, similar methods have indicated that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Kriszt et al., 2017), cell nucleus (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), plasma membrane (Liang et al., 2022), and different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons (Tanimoto et al., 2016), are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kriszt et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The cell nucleus is at a temperature distinct from the extracellular environment.
claims.source: In addition, similar methods have indicated that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Kriszt et al., 2017), cell nucleus (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), plasma membrane (Liang et al., 2022), and different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons (Tanimoto et al., 2016), are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Okabe et al., 2012 and Hayashi et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The plasma membrane is at a temperature distinct from the extracellular environment.
claims.source: In addition, similar methods have indicated that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Kriszt et al., 2017), cell nucleus (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), plasma membrane (Liang et al., 2022), and different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons (Tanimoto et al., 2016), are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons, are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
claims.source: In addition, similar methods have indicated that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Kriszt et al., 2017), cell nucleus (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), plasma membrane (Liang et al., 2022), and different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons (Tanimoto et al., 2016), are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tanimoto et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The cells of many organisms, notably homeotherms, are unable to tolerate prolonged high or low temperatures when applied externally.
claims.source: In particular, since the cells of many organisms, notably homeotherms, are unable to tolerate prolonged high or low temperatures when applied externally, the question arises as to how much the temperature of mitochondria is permitted to vary in vivo, and whether and how it is regulated according to physiological conditions (Lane, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular temperature tolerance, with a citation to Lane, 2018 for context.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial temperature is physiologically maintained at ~15°C above ambient temperature.
claims.source: Broadly, the outcome of these studies verifies that mitochondrial temperature is physiologically maintained at ~15°C above ambient temperature, and is subject to homeostatic regulation in response to metabolic stress.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript using MTY and gTEMP methods.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial temperature is subject to homeostatic regulation in response to metabolic stress.
claims.source: Broadly, the outcome of these studies verifies that mitochondrial temperature is physiologically maintained at ~15°C above ambient temperature, and is subject to homeostatic regulation in response to metabolic stress.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing temperature maintenance under various metabolic stresses, as shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claims.claim: The fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature.
claims.source: These trials showed that the fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), or pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), across the physiological range of these parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: MTY fluorescence is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration across the physiological range.
claims.source: These trials showed that the fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), or pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), across the physiological range of these parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: MTY fluorescence is not responsive to changes in hydrogen peroxide across the physiological range.
claims.source: These trials showed that the fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), or pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), across the physiological range of these parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: MTY fluorescence is not responsive to changes in pH across the physiological range.
claims.source: These trials showed that the fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), or pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), across the physiological range of these parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claims.claim: In most cell lines tested there was a clear gradation of mitochondrial temperature decrease using inhibitors that act progressively further along the OXPHOS chain: the effect was always greatest after oligomycin and generally least for rotenone, with potassium cyanide and antimycin intermediate.
claims.source: In most cell lines tested there was a clear gradation of mitochondrial temperature decrease using inhibitors that act progressively further along the OXPHOS chain: the effect was always greatest after oligomycin (inhibitor of cV) and generally least for rotenone (cI inhibitor), with potassium cyanide (inhibitor of OXPHOS complex IV, cIV) and antimycin (cIII inhibitor) intermediate (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 across multiple cell lines.

claims.claim: Oligomycin produced an implied temperature decrease of the order of 17–19°C in most cell lines.
claims.source: In general, findings were similar for different cell lines, with an implied temperature decrease of the order of 17–19°C produced by oligomycin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from MTY fluorescence measurements across multiple cell lines, as shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Oligomycin-induced temperature decrease implies a mitochondrial temperature of at least 54°C, assuming that cV inhibition abolishes all mitochondrial heat production.
claims.source: This implies a mitochondrial temperature of at least 54°C, assuming that cV inhibition abolishes all mitochondrial heat production, ±2°C, taking account of the possible slight deviation from linearity seen in the MTY fluorescence temperature-response curve at higher temperatures (dotted line, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and the assumption about oligomycin's effect, with reference to the calibration curve.

claims.claim: Two different isolates of immortalised mouse embryonic fibroblasts (iMEFs) gave similar results in mitochondrial temperature measurements.
claims.source: Two different isolates of immortalised mouse embryonic fibroblasts (iMEFs) gave similar results (Figure 2C and D), with no significant difference in the extent of mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone to inhibit cI or by antimycin to inhibit cIII (Figure 2C and D) or by a combination of the two drugs (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing two iMEF lines, as shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the extent of mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone or antimycin in two iMEF isolates.
claims.source: Two different isolates of immortalised mouse embryonic fibroblasts (iMEFs) gave similar results (Figure 2C and D), with no significant difference in the extent of mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone to inhibit cI or by antimycin to inhibit cIII (Figure 2C and D) or by a combination of the two drugs (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: The inferred temperature of mitochondria in S2 cells from Drosophila, when suspended and oxygenated at 25°C, showed similar responses to OXPHOS inhibition as mammalian cells suspended at 37°C, except for oligomycin treatment.
claims.source: The inferred temperature of mitochondria in S2 cells from the fruit-fly Drosophila, a poikilotherm, when suspended and oxygenated at 25°C, showed similar responses to OXPHOS inhibition as mammalian cells suspended at 37°C, except that we were unable to derive a stable reading after oligomycin treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D, panel i).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from S2 cells, as shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5D.

claims.claim: MTY fluorescence was still increasing 2 hr after the addition of oligomycin to S2 cells, whereas other inhibitors gave a stable reading over the same time period.
claims.source: MTY fluorescence was still increasing 2 hr after the addition of oligomycin, whereas other inhibitors, such as KCN, when applied to S2 cells, gave a stable reading over the same time period (e.g. Figure 2—figure supplement 5D, panel ii).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5D.

claims.claim: Fluorescence reached a stable value after the addition of oligomycin in all cell lines tested except S2 cells.
claims.source: Fluorescence reached a stable value after the addition of oligomycin in all of the other cell lines tested, e.g., U2OS human osteosarcoma cells as shown (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D, panel iii).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations across multiple cell lines, with U2OS shown as an example in Figure 2—figure supplement 5D, panel iii.

claims.claim: Overnight growth in media predicted to stimulate mitochondrial as opposed to cytosolic ATP production had no effect on mitochondrial temperature.
claims.source: We investigated the effect of culturing iMEF cells in low-glucose medium, with or without galactose supplementation, aiming to enhance dependence on mitochondrial respiration (Marroquin et al., 2007). This culture-medium alteration produced no significant change to the effect of cI inhibition on mitochondrial temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, with citation to Marroquin et al., 2007 for the rationale.

claims.claim: The fluorescence of Sirius is highly temperature sensitive, declining as temperature rises, whereas that of mT-Sapphire is not.
claims.source: The basis of the method is the fact that the fluorescence of Sirius is highly temperature sensitive, declining (like MTY) as temperature rises, whereas that of mT-Sapphire is not.
claims.evidence: This describes the fundamental principle of the mito-gTEMP temperature measurement method, based on established knowledge from Nakano et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The peak fluorescence ratio of mito-gTEMP is independent of expression level.
claims.source: Since the two proteins are expressed at a fixed stoichiometry, the peak fluorescence ratio is independent of expression level, which may vary even within a cloned mammalian cell population (Pilbrough et al., 2009), as seen, for example, in Figure 3B.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the design of the mito-gTEMP construct and is supported by citation to Pilbrough et al., 2009 regarding expression variability, with visual evidence in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Oligomycin treatment of mito-gTEMP-expressing cell clones derived from three different mammalian cell lines gave extrapolated values for the mitochondrial temperature decrease in the same range as those inferred by MTY, although slightly (1–2°C) less in each case.
claims.source: Oligomycin treatment of mito-gTEMP-expressing cell clones derived from three different mammalian cell lines gave extrapolated values for the mitochondrial temperature decrease in the same range as those inferred by MTY, although slightly (1–2°C) less in each case, implying an internal mitochondrial matrix temperature of ~52–54°C (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing MTY and mito-gTEMP methods across three cell lines, as shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The internal mitochondrial matrix temperature is ~52–54°C based on mito-gTEMP measurements.
claims.source: Oligomycin treatment of mito-gTEMP-expressing cell clones derived from three different mammalian cell lines gave extrapolated values for the mitochondrial temperature decrease in the same range as those inferred by MTY, although slightly (1–2°C) less in each case, implying an internal mitochondrial matrix temperature of ~52–54°C (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from mito-gTEMP measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Rotenone treatment of iMEF(P) cells produced a similar amount of mitochondrial temperature decrease when estimated by mito-gTEMP as by MTY.
claims.source: Rotenone treatment of iMEF(P) cells also produced a similar amount of mitochondrial temperature decrease when estimated by mito-gTEMP as by MTY (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the two methods in rotenone-treated cells, as shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The matrix localisation of GFP-related fluorescent reporters using the COX8 targeting peptide is well documented.
claims.source: The matrix localisation of GFP-related fluorescent reporters using the COX8 targeting peptide is well documented (Molina and Shirihai, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Molina and Shirihai, 2009.

claims.claim: At least some MTY interacts with the matrix protein aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2).
claims.source: However, the exact intramitochondrial location of MTY is not known, besides the fact that at least some of it interacts with the matrix protein aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) (Arai et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arai et al., 2015.

claims.claim: In mitochondrial subfractionation experiments, the mean proportion of MTY fluorescence retained in mitoplasts was 92%.
claims.source: In the first fractionation step, mitoplasts were separated from the outer membrane space/IMS fraction. In two trials, the mean proportion of MTY fluorescence retained in mitoplasts was 92%.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mitochondrial subfractionation experiments.

claims.claim: In mitochondrial subfractionation experiments, the mean proportion of MTY fluorescence retained in the SMP fraction was 90%.
claims.source: In the second fractionation step, mitoplasts were sonicated to prepare fractions enriched for matrix versus 'inside-out' sub-mitochondrial particles (SMPs). In two trials, the mean proportion of MTY fluorescence retained in the SMP fraction was 90%.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mitochondrial subfractionation experiments.

claims.claim: MTY is retained within, or closely associated with, the inner mitochondrial membrane.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with MTY being retained within, or closely associated with, the inner mitochondrial membrane.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the subfractionation data showing MTY retention in SMPs.

claims.claim: Mitochondria in individual cells were cooled to variable extents by oligomycin treatment.
claims.source: Time-lapse imaging revealed that mitochondria in individual cells were cooled to variable extents by oligomycin treatment (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: When mito-gTEMP-expressing iMEF cells were incubated in PBS at 37°C without any inhibitor, there was a modest but progressive decline in the fluorescence ratio over 35 min, indicating mitochondrial temperature was around 4°C lower than the peak value reached at approximately 10 min.
claims.source: When mito-gTEMP-expressing iMEF cells were incubated in PBS at 37°C without the addition of any inhibitor, we observed that, after reaching a steady fluorescence ratio indicative of a temperature of 53–54°C, there was a modest but progressive decline in the fluorescence ratio, such that by 35 min of incubation the inferred mitochondrial temperature was around 4°C lower than the peak value reached at approximately 10 min (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: In the complete absence of an externally supplied, metabolisable substrate, mitochondrial metabolism adjusts to a slightly lower heat output and steady-state temperature.
claims.source: Although remaining much warmer than the surrounding medium, this suggests that, in the complete absence of an externally supplied, metabolisable substrate, mitochondrial metabolism adjusts to a slightly lower heat output and steady-state temperature.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of temperature decline in PBS without substrates.

claims.claim: The addition of glucose and glutamine enabled mitochondria to maintain a higher temperature of ~53°C at the end of the experiment.
claims.source: As expected, this enabled mitochondria to maintain a higher temperature of ~53°C at the end of the experiment, although this was still slightly less than the initial temperature peak of ~55°C between 5 and 10 min of incubation (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: The addition of glucose and glutamine at 10 min produced a small rise in mitochondrial temperature.
claims.source: However, the addition of glucose and glutamine at 10 min did produce a small rise in mitochondrial temperature (Figure 5B and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and D.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial temperature fluctuates within a narrow range according to substrate supply.
claims.source: In sum, these data indicate that mitochondrial temperature fluctuates within a narrow range according to substrate supply.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing temperature changes with substrate addition and removal.

claims.claim: Cultured mouse fibroblasts respond to BKA by inducing glycolysis and downregulating mitochondrial respiration, whilst maintaining a high mitochondrial membrane potential.
claims.source: Previous investigators have shown that cultured mouse fibroblasts respond to BKA by inducing glycolysis and downregulating mitochondrial respiration, whilst maintaining a high mitochondrial membrane potential (Kano et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kano et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The mitochondrial temperature decrease observed after BKA treatment was minimal, following an apparent slight increase upon addition of the drug.
claims.source: However, the mitochondrial temperature decrease that we observed was minimal, following an apparent slight increase upon addition of the drug (Figure 5E and F), qualitatively consistent with the MTY signal after discounting the quenching effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In cells that principally metabolise cI-linked substrates, AOX makes only a minor contribution to respiratory electron flow under non-inhibited conditions.
claims.source: In cells that principally metabolise cI-linked substrates, AOX makes only a minor contribution to respiratory electron flow under non-inhibited conditions (Szibor et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szibor et al., 2020.

claims.claim: If cI is blocked, forcing cells to switch to other ubiquinone-linked substrates, AOX becomes engaged.
claims.source: However, if cI is blocked, forcing cells to switch to other ubiquinone-linked substrates, AOX becomes engaged (Szibor et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szibor et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The initial mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone in AOX-expressing iMEFs was very similar to that of control iMEFs.
claims.source: Consistent with these expectations, the initial mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by the cI inhibitor rotenone in AOX-expressing iMEFs was very similar to that of control iMEFs, with a mitochondrial temperature decrease of ~10°C based on both MTY fluorescence (Figure 6A, panel i, Figure 6B) and the mito-gTEMP fluorescence ratio measured in iMEF cells stably transfected with AOX (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: After the initial temperature decrease from rotenone, AOX-expressing iMEFs showed gradual mitochondrial rewarming.
claims.source: However, this was followed by a gradual mitochondrial rewarming (Figure 6A, panel i, Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, panel ii).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: AOX-expressing iMEFs treated with other OXPHOS inhibitors showed a similar rewarming behaviour, except that the initial mitochondrial temperature decrease was substantially less than that seen in control iMEFs.
claims.source: AOX-expressing iMEFs treated with other OXPHOS inhibitors showed a similar behaviour (Figure 6A panels ii–iv, Figure 6C), except that the initial mitochondrial temperature decrease was substantially less than that seen in control iMEFs (Figure 6A panels ii–iv, Figure 6B), whilst the rate and extent of rewarming differed according to the inhibitor used (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: The rate and extent of mitochondrial rewarming in AOX-expressing iMEFs differed according to the inhibitor used.
claims.source: AOX-expressing iMEFs treated with other OXPHOS inhibitors showed a similar behaviour (Figure 6A panels ii–iv, Figure 6C), except that the initial mitochondrial temperature decrease was substantially less than that seen in control iMEFs (Figure 6A panels ii–iv, Figure 6B), whilst the rate and extent of rewarming differed according to the inhibitor used (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Anisomycin treatment led to a transient slight increase in mitochondrial temperature (~4°C).
claims.source: In contrast to our expectation that anisomycin, by attenuating ATP demand, would decrease electron flux in the OXPHOS system and thus lead to a drop in mitochondrial temperature, the latter instead showed a transient slight increase (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: High mitochondrial temperature was sustained for many hours after anisomycin treatment.
claims.source: Thereafter, high mitochondrial temperature was sustained for many hours, although by 18 hr of exposure to the drug many of the cells were no longer attached and probably dying (the cells analysed in Figure 7A were those that had remained attached).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: AOX-expressing iMEF cells remained healthy-looking even after 18 hr in anisomycin.
claims.source: AOX-expressing iMEF cells (Figure 7B) showed an almost identical behaviour, except that the cells remained healthy-looking even after 18 hr in anisomycin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The inferred mitochondrial temperature of anisomycin-treated iMEFs showed a lesser effect of rotenone than iMEFs not treated with anisomycin, and this effect was increasingly pronounced after longer times of anisomycin exposure.
claims.source: The inferred mitochondrial temperature of anisomycin-treated iMEFs showed a lesser effect of rotenone than iMEFs not treated with anisomycin (Figure 7C, blue trace, compare 1–18 hr time-points with 0 hr control), and this effect was increasingly pronounced after longer times of anisomycin exposure.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial temperature in surviving cells after 18 hr in anisomycin was almost unaffected by rotenone.
claims.source: Mitochondrial temperature in the surviving cells after 18 hr in anisomycin was almost unaffected by rotenone.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Anisomycin-exposed iMEFs were as affected by oligomycin as prior to treatment, even up to 18 hr.
claims.source: In contrast, and despite some experiment-to-experiment variation, anisomycin-exposed iMEFs were as affected by oligomycin as prior to treatment, even up to 18 hr (Figure 7D, blue trace).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: After anisomycin treatment, AOX-expressing iMEFs showed a consistently greater mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone than did control iMEFs not expressing AOX.
claims.source: AOX-expressing iMEFs behaved differently. After anisomycin treatment, they showed a consistently greater mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone (Figure 7C, red trace) than did control iMEFs not expressing AOX (Figure 7C, blue trace).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The mitochondria of anisomycin-treated iMEF(AOX) cells showed a temperature decrease by oligomycin significantly less than anisomycin-treated control iMEF(P) cells, regardless of the length of time of anisomycin exposure.
claims.source: The mitochondria of anisomycin-treated iMEF(AOX) cells showed a temperature decrease by oligomycin significantly less than anisomycin-treated control iMEF(P) cells, regardless of the length of time of anisomycin exposure, but also showed a possibly increased effect of oligomycin, with increasing anisomycin exposure time (Figure 7D, red trace), at least for the first hours.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Anisomycin-exposed iMEF(AOX) cells showed the same slow rewarming after rotenone treatment as did iMEF(AOX) cells not exposed to anisomycin.
claims.source: Anisomycin-exposed iMEF(AOX) cells showed the same slow rewarming after rotenone treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, panel i) as did iMEF(AOX) cells not exposed to anisomycin (Figure 6A panel i, Figure 6C), whilst control iMEFs did not show any such effect from rotenone (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, panel ii).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6.

claims.claim: The rewarming effect after oligomycin treatment was slower and of much lower magnitude for anisomycin-treated than untreated iMEF(AOX) cells.
claims.source: Conversely, the rewarming effect after oligomycin treatment was slower and of much lower magnitude for anisomycin-treated than untreated iMEF(AOX) cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), whilst a modest rewarming was also seen for control iMEFs not expressing AOX (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Much of the heat generated by OXPHOS is retained within the organelle, keeping mitochondrial temperature far above that of other cell components.
claims.source: Our findings are inconsistent with this model, indicating instead that much of the heat generated by OXPHOS is retained within the organelle, keeping mitochondrial temperature far above that of other cell components and, whenever possible, within a narrow range.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings of high mitochondrial temperature.

claims.claim: Heat conductance from the mitochondria might be modulated to maintain mitochondrial temperature.
claims.source: Heat conductance from the mitochondria might also be modulated to maintain mitochondrial temperature.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism for temperature regulation.

claims.claim: The use of a Peltier jacket surrounding the cuvette ensures that temperature changes in the cuvette rapidly and accurately reflect those applied.
claims.source: The use of a Peltier jacket surrounding the cuvette in the apparatus ensures that temperature changes in the cuvette rapidly and accurately reflect those applied, as verified (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by validation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The MTY-based measurements may be slightly in error (by ~2°C), due to the minor deviation from linearity of the MTY fluorescence temperature-response curve, in the inferred temperature range of 50–60°C.
claims.source: As stated earlier, the MTY-based measurements may be slightly in error (by ~2°C), due to the minor deviation from linearity of the MTY fluorescence temperature-response curve, in the inferred temperature range of 50–60°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the calibration data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Drugs that have different effects on mitochondrial membrane potential nevertheless all lead to a sustained increase in MTY fluorescence.
claims.source: In previous studies it was argued that drugs that have different effects on mitochondrial membrane potential nevertheless all lead to a sustained increase in MTY fluorescence.
claims.evidence: This refers to arguments made in previous studies, likely Chrétien et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Treatment of cells with respiratory inhibitors such as rotenone or antimycin lead to substantially decreased membrane potential.
claims.source: Treatment of cells with respiratory inhibitors such as rotenone or antimycin lead to substantially decreased membrane potential (Cannino et al., 2012; Kalbácová et al., 2003), whereas the effects of oligomycin on mitochondrial membrane potential are generally minor, and vary between cell lines and over time.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cannino et al., 2012 and Kalbácová et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The effects of oligomycin on mitochondrial membrane potential are generally minor, and vary between cell lines and over time.
claims.source: Treatment of cells with respiratory inhibitors such as rotenone or antimycin lead to substantially decreased membrane potential (Cannino et al., 2012; Kalbácová et al., 2003), whereas the effects of oligomycin on mitochondrial membrane potential are generally minor, and vary between cell lines and over time.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Kalbácová et al., 2003 and Yang et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Oligomycin commonly results in a small increase in mitochondrial membrane potential, sometimes followed by a decrease.
claims.source: Commonly, oligomycin results in a small increase in mitochondrial membrane potential, sometimes followed by a decrease (Kalbácová et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kalbácová et al., 2003 and Yang et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Any quantitative effect of membrane potential on MTY fluorescence is negligible, unless the potential is completely lost, leading to dye leakage.
claims.source: This implies that any quantitative effect of membrane potential on MTY fluorescence is negligible, unless the potential is completely lost, leading to dye leakage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and comparison with membrane potential studies.

claims.claim: The excitation wavelength for gTEMP (360 nm) falls within the ultraviolet range, and the resulting cellular damage under continuous illumination for more than 60 min renders calibration unreliable.

results.result: Active mitochondria in mammalian and insect cell lines maintain temperatures approximately 15°C above ambient (52-54°C in mammalian cells at 37°C), as measured by both MTY fluorescence and mito-gTEMP ratiometric indicators. Oligomycin treatment produced temperature decreases of 17-19°C, implying baseline mitochondrial temperatures of at least 54°C.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C22, C29, C30, C40, and C41 are well-supported by convergent evidence from two independent measurement methods (MTY and mito-gTEMP) across multiple cell lines (C1, C28, C31, C40). The temperature estimates are based on systematic calibration procedures (C74, C83) and show consistent results across methods, though with acknowledged measurement uncertainties of ±2°C (C75). The use of two independent fluorescent methods strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: MTY fluorescence decreases almost linearly with temperature and is not responsive to physiological changes in calcium, hydrogen peroxide, or pH. The Peltier-controlled apparatus ensures accurate temperature control, though measurements may have ~2°C error at 50-60°C due to slight non-linearity.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 and C74 are directly supported by experimental validation data (Figures 2—figure supplements 2-4). The acknowledgment of potential measurement error (C75) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution. These validation experiments are essential controls that strengthen confidence in the temperature measurements.

results.result: The mito-gTEMP ratiometric temperature indicator, based on temperature-sensitive Sirius and temperature-insensitive mT-Sapphire fluorescent proteins, provides expression-independent temperature measurements that corroborate MTY findings. However, calibration above 42°C requires extrapolation due to cellular viability limits.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 are supported by experimental data (Figure 3) and appropriate citations (C43). The methodological limitation requiring extrapolation above 42°C (C83, C84) is transparently acknowledged. The concordance between MTY and mito-gTEMP measurements (C40, C42) provides important cross-validation, though the 1-2°C systematic difference requires explanation.

results.result: Different OXPHOS inhibitors produce a graded pattern of mitochondrial temperature decrease (oligomycin > KCN > antimycin ≥ rotenone), reflecting the proportion of electron flow entering at each step. Cell-line specific differences reveal varying contributions from alternative electron entry pathways.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 is directly supported by systematic data across cell lines (Figure 2). The inferences about electron flow pathways (C97-C101) are logical deductions from the inhibitor data, though some (C99) could not be directly verified with MitoBloCK-6. The pattern is internally consistent and biologically plausible, representing careful interpretation of the experimental results.

results.result: Mitochondrial subfractionation experiments show that 92% of MTY fluorescence is retained in mitoplasts and 90% in sub-mitochondrial particles (SMPs), indicating MTY localizes to or near the inner mitochondrial membrane rather than the matrix.
results.evaluation: Claims C45 and C46 report experimental data from subfractionation (n=2 trials each). While the sample size is small, the results are consistent and the inference (C47) is reasonable. This localization difference from mito-gTEMP (which targets to matrix) may explain the 1-2°C temperature difference between methods and is important for interpretation.

results.result: Mitochondrial temperature is maintained during substrate starvation, declining only modestly (~4°C over 35 min) in PBS without substrates. Addition of glucose and glutamine restores or maintains higher temperatures, indicating temperature fluctuates within a narrow range according to substrate supply.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by mito-gTEMP measurements (Figure 5A-D). The data show clear substrate-dependent temperature modulation while maintaining temperatures well above ambient. This demonstrates homeostatic regulation rather than passive heat dissipation, supporting the broader claim C2 about temperature maintenance under metabolic stress.

results.result: Inhibition of the adenine nucleotide transporter with BKA produced minimal mitochondrial temperature decrease despite inducing metabolic switching to glycolysis, suggesting intramitochondrial ATP turnover can maintain near-normal heat production.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by experimental data (Figure 5E-F), but the mechanistic interpretation (C112) is speculative. The minimal temperature change is surprising given the expected metabolic effects (C54), and the proposed mechanism of boosted intramitochondrial ATP turnover lacks direct experimental support. Additional experiments measuring intramitochondrial ATP levels and turnover would be needed to support the mechanistic claims.

results.result: In cells expressing alternative oxidase (AOX), mitochondrial temperature is initially decreased by OXPHOS inhibitors but then gradually rewarms over 40-70 minutes. This rewarming requires metabolic switching to flavin-linked substrates that reduce ubiquinone, bypassing the inhibited complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are well-supported by experimental data (Figure 6) showing the rewarming phenomenon. The mechanistic interpretations (C102-C107, C109-C110) are logical inferences supported by appropriate citations (C56, C57, C104-C106) and consistent with known AOX biochemistry. However, the exact metabolic changes underlying rewarming (C109) remain speculative and would benefit from metabolomic analysis. The evolutionary/ecological speculation (C108) is reasonable but extends beyond the data.

results.result: Inhibition of cytosolic protein synthesis with anisomycin, which should reduce ATP demand by 35-70%, paradoxically maintained high mitochondrial temperature for many hours. Over time, temperature maintenance became less dependent on complex I but remained fully dependent on ATP synthase, suggesting a shift toward thermogenic ATP hydrolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C71 are supported by systematic time-course data (Figure 7). The finding is surprising and contradicts initial expectations, which strengthens confidence it is not an artifact. However, the mechanistic interpretations (C114-C118) are largely speculative. The proposed mechanisms involving ATP synthase operating as an ATPase (C115) and futile cycles (C116-C117) lack direct experimental support and represent hypotheses requiring further testing.

results.result: The authors propose that high mitochondrial temperature is an inescapable consequence of OXPHOS biochemistry and is homeostatically maintained as a primary feature of mitochondrial metabolism, requiring robust and flexible mechanisms for heat flow regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C23, and C146 represent the central thesis supported by the collective experimental evidence of temperature maintenance under diverse metabolic stresses (C2-C5, C62-C71). The inference that heat is retained within mitochondria (C72) is supported by the temperature measurements. However, claims about specific regulatory mechanisms (C73, C120, C121) remain speculative. The proposal is well-supported as a general principle but mechanistic details require further investigation.

results.result: The effect of membrane potential on MTY fluorescence is negligible unless potential is completely lost, as evidenced by the fact that inhibitors with different effects on membrane potential all produce sustained MTY fluorescence increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are supported by appropriate citations to parallel studies of membrane potential. The inference (C80) that membrane potential effects are negligible is logical given that inhibitors with opposite effects on membrane potential (rotenone/antimycin decrease it, oligomycin may increase it) all increase MTY fluorescence. This is an important control addressing a potential confounding variable.

results.result: The UV excitation wavelength (360 nm) for gTEMP causes cellular damage under continuous illumination beyond 60 minutes, limiting calibration reliability. The recently developed B-gTEMP should overcome this limitation in future studies.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2022, and explains why mito-gTEMP measurements were limited to 35 minutes. This is an important methodological limitation that prevented long-term temperature tracking. The suggestion about B-gTEMP (C82) is appropriately framed as future work.

results.result: Despite theoretical and experimental challenges to high mitochondrial temperature, recent data on slow thermal diffusivity in mammalian cells and theoretical work by Fahimi and Matta on proton-mediated heat transfer provide physical explanations consistent with the experimental findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 appropriately acknowledge challenges and cite supporting theoretical work. Claims C122-C127 discuss the Fahimi and Matta theoretical framework with appropriate citations. The evaluation (C125) that this is the only physically sound hypothesis may be overstated, but the theoretical support strengthens the plausibility of the experimental findings. This represents appropriate engagement with theoretical considerations.

results.result: The double membrane system of mitochondria may serve as thermal insulation, and mitochondrial fusion/fission dynamics may be regulated by temperature homeostasis, with fragmentation occurring when heat output rises or is abolished, and fusion when heat output is low.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C132 are speculative inferences from the temperature data. Supporting evidence from the literature (C133-C139) shows correlations between OXPHOS inhibition, mitochondrial dynamics, and temperature changes, but causation is not established. The hypothesis is plausible and testable but requires direct experimental manipulation of mitochondrial temperature independent of metabolic state to establish causality. The observation about U2OS cells (C137) provides correlative support but is insufficient for strong conclusions.

results.result: OXPHOS complexes have temperature optima around 50-55°C in intact membranes and respiratory chain proteins have melting temperatures around 60°C, consistent with high mitochondrial temperature. However, externally applied heat above 43°C damages mitochondria, implying heat production must be finely regulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 and C96 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. The inference (C94-C95) that mitochondria already at elevated temperature are vulnerable to external heating is logical and important for understanding why cells cannot tolerate high external temperatures despite high internal mitochondrial temperatures. This reconciles an apparent paradox in the findings.

results.result: The authors predict that bacterial OXPHOS systems should produce similar heat, resulting in intracellular temperatures 15-20°C above ambient, and that loss of mitochondrial heat generation in disease may have profound metabolic consequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C145 are speculative extrapolations from the current findings. The bacterial prediction (C142-C143) is logical given the evolutionary origin of mitochondria but requires experimental verification. The disease implications (C144-C145) are plausible but highly speculative without direct evidence from disease models. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future investigation but are not supported by the current data.

results.result: Background claims establish that OXPHOS is thermodynamically inefficient, producing substantial heat under normal conditions that contributes to thermoregulation in homeotherms. Previous studies using MTY and protein-based probes have indicated high mitochondrial temperatures and temperature heterogeneity across cellular compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C21 represent established knowledge and prior work, appropriately cited throughout (C9-C13, C14-C20). These provide essential context for the current study and are accurately represented. The citations support the claims made about OXPHOS efficiency, heat production, thermoregulation, and prior temperature measurements.

results.result: Two independent iMEF isolates showed similar mitochondrial temperature responses to inhibitors, with no significant differences between rotenone and antimycin effects. Drosophila S2 cells showed similar responses except for unstable oligomycin readings. Culture medium modifications did not affect mitochondrial temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 demonstrate reproducibility across independent cell isolates (Figure 2C-D). The S2 cell findings (C33-C35) identify a cell-line specific technical limitation transparently reported. The culture medium experiment (C36) provides a negative control showing temperature is not simply determined by metabolic substrate availability. These claims support the robustness and generalizability of the findings.

results.result: Time-lapse imaging revealed that mitochondria in individual cells were cooled to variable extents by oligomycin treatment, indicating heterogeneity in mitochondrial temperature responses within cell populations.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by time-lapse imaging data (Figure 4C). This observation of cell-to-cell heterogeneity is important for understanding the biological variability in the system and suggests that mitochondrial temperature may be regulated at the individual organelle or cell level. The finding adds biological context to the population-averaged measurements.

results.result: Bright puncta observed in MTY-stained cells may correspond to nucleoids, as the ALDH2 orthologue in yeast is a nucleoid protein, though this has not been reported in mammals.
results.evaluation: Claim C140 is speculative based on microscopy observations (Figure 4B). The supporting evidence from yeast (C141) is appropriately cited but the authors acknowledge this has not been shown in mammals. The bright puncta could represent cooler regions, preferential dye binding, or artifacts. This observation is interesting but requires further investigation with nucleoid markers and additional controls.

results.result: The authors claim that mitochondrial temperature in cultured cells is maintained at approximately 15°C above ambient temperature (up to 50-54°C), based on measurements using MTY and mito-gTEMP fluorescent probes across multiple cell lines. This represents the central finding of the manuscript.
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed significant concerns about the methodology and interpretation. One reviewer stated the methodology 'is not well-established to begin with and requires additional controls for interpretation' and noted 'very little benchmarking is done of the basal fluorescence ratio.' Another reviewer acknowledged 'the evidence supporting the hypothesis is solid' but noted that 'direct measures of temperature in isolated mitochondria or comparison with other cellular compartments would have strengthened the ability to interpret the relevance of the findings.' A third reviewer stated the authors 'did not achieve their Aims to accurately determine the temperature of mitochondria' and that 'the results, while interesting, are preliminary and require additional controls before conclusions can be drawn.'

results.result: The authors report that mito-gTEMP measurements gave similar temperature estimates to MTY (52-54°C for mitochondrial matrix temperature), with values 1-2°C lower than MTY across three cell lines, providing independent validation of the MTY findings.
results.evaluation: One reviewer acknowledged as a strength that 'demonstration that both a fluorescent (Mito Thermo Yellow) and a genetic-based (mito-gTEMP) mitochondrial targeted temperature probe elicit similar quantitative changes in mitochondrial temperature under different experimental conditions' and that 'the addition of the genetic probe to the current study supports prior findings using the fluorescent probe.' However, another reviewer raised concerns that 'the authors do not rigorously control for other factors that may also be changing fluorescence and may be confounders to the delta fluorescence (eg, delta calcium in response to mito inhibitors, membrane potential, redox status, ROS, etc.)' and that calibration issues remain unresolved.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that MTY fluorescence in cell-free solution decreases linearly with temperature and is not responsive to changes in calcium, hydrogen peroxide, or pH across physiological ranges, supporting its specificity as a temperature probe.
results.evaluation: While these control experiments are presented, one reviewer specifically criticized that 'the authors do not rigorously control for other factors that may also be changing fluorescence and may be confounders' and requested 'additional calibration for all potential confounders.' Another reviewer noted the need for 'comparison with other cellular compartments' to validate that only mitochondria appear hot, suggesting the controls provided are insufficient.

results.result: The authors report a gradation of mitochondrial temperature decrease with different OXPHOS inhibitors, with oligomycin (cV inhibitor) producing the greatest effect (17-19°C), suggesting that ATP synthase itself generates heat even in the absence of respiration through ATP hydrolysis.
results.evaluation: One reviewer noted as a strength that 'the authors couple these measurements with other perturbation of mitochondria, such as OXPHOS inhibitors, to show consistency.' However, another reviewer raised a critical weakness: 'the severity of the interventions (e.g., mitochondrial complex-specific inhibitors, inhibition of protein synthesis) and the absence of simultaneous or parallel measurements of other key bioenergetic parameters (i.e., membrane potential, oxygen consumption rate, etc.) limits the ability to interpret potential cause and effect.' The inference about ATP synthase-mediated heat generation is not directly validated.

results.result: The authors claim that high mitochondrial temperature is maintained under various metabolic stresses including substrate starvation, inhibition of ATP demand, and inhibition of adenine nucleotide transport, demonstrating homeostatic regulation of mitochondrial temperature.
results.evaluation: One reviewer acknowledged that 'additional evidence shows that mitochondria maintain higher temperatures under several different types of cellular metabolic stresses predicted to decrease the dependence on OxPhos, adding to the notion that natural thermodynamic inefficiency and heat generation may be an important, and potentially regulated, characteristic of mitochondrial metabolism.' However, the same reviewer noted a critical weakness: 'several of the interventions are employed to either increase or decrease dependence on OxPhos flux, but no outcome measures are reported to document whether the intended objective was achieved (e.g., increased OxPhos flux in low glucose plus galactose, decreased ATP demand-OxPhos flux with anisomycin, etc.)' This limits confidence in the homeostatic regulation interpretation.

results.result: In AOX-expressing cells, the authors report that after initial temperature decrease from OXPHOS inhibitors, mitochondria show gradual rewarming, with the rate and extent depending on the inhibitor used, suggesting metabolic flexibility in maintaining mitochondrial temperature.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the experimental design, one noted the critical limitation that 'the absence of simultaneous or parallel measurements of other key bioenergetic parameters (i.e., membrane potential, oxygen consumption rate, etc.) limits the ability to interpret potential cause and effect - whether the thermogenesis aspect of OxPhos is being sensed and regulated, or whether temperature changes are more of a biproduct of adjustments in OxPhos flux.' The rewarming phenomenon is documented but its mechanistic interpretation remains uncertain without supporting metabolic measurements.

results.result: The authors report that anisomycin treatment (inhibiting cytosolic protein synthesis) led to sustained high mitochondrial temperature with altered responses to OXPHOS inhibitors over time, with differences between control and AOX-expressing cells.
results.evaluation: One reviewer specifically noted the weakness that 'several of the interventions are employed to either increase or decrease dependence on OxPhos flux, but no outcome measures are reported to document whether the intended objective was achieved (e.g., increased OxPhos flux in low glucose plus galactose, decreased ATP demand-OxPhos flux with anisomycin, etc.)' Without confirmation that anisomycin actually decreased ATP demand as intended, the interpretation of these temperature changes remains uncertain.

results.result: The authors propose that high mitochondrial temperature is an inescapable consequence of OXPHOS biochemistry and is homeostatically maintained as a primary feature of mitochondrial metabolism, representing a novel paradigm for understanding mitochondrial function.
results.evaluation: One reviewer noted 'the physiological relevance of the findings remains unclear' given the methodological limitations. Another reviewer stated that while the study 'provides useful data supporting prior findings,' it 'does not substantially clarify the true temperature of mitochondria or resolve potential discrepancies in previous estimates.' The broader interpretive framework proposed by the authors is not directly evaluated by reviewers but is undermined by concerns about the foundational temperature measurements.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that mito-gTEMP calibration required extrapolation beyond 42°C (assuming linearity) because in vivo calibration above this temperature is not possible due to loss of cellular viability.
results.evaluation: This methodological limitation is explicitly acknowledged by the authors and represents a transparent discussion of the constraints of the method. Reviewers did not dispute this limitation but rather emphasized it as part of broader concerns about calibration and validation.

results.result: Mitochondrial subfractionation experiments showed that 92% of MTY fluorescence was retained in mitoplasts and 90% in sub-mitochondrial particles (SMPs), suggesting MTY is retained within or closely associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane.
results.evaluation: These localization data are presented as supporting evidence for MTY's mitochondrial specificity. While reviewers raised broader concerns about probe validation, they did not specifically challenge these subfractionation results. One reviewer did request experiments with 'isolated mitochondria and other isolated organelles' to clarify specificity, suggesting these data alone are insufficient but not incorrect.

comparisons.comparison: Both address core temperature measurement claims (C1, C22, C29, C30). OpenEval finds claims well-supported by convergent evidence from two methods, while peer reviewers express significant uncertainty about methodology, noting it 'is not well-established' and 'requires additional controls.' Major disagreement on whether the evidence is sufficient.

Both evaluate validation/control experiments (C24-C27). OpenEval finds these validation experiments strengthen confidence in measurements, while peer reviewers find them insufficient, requesting 'additional calibration for all potential confounders' and noting authors 'do not rigorously control for other factors.' Disagreement on adequacy of controls.

Both discuss concordance between MTY and mito-gTEMP methods (C40, C42). OpenEval finds cross-validation provides important support despite 1-2°C difference. Peer reviewers acknowledge this as a strength ('supports prior findings') but raise concerns about uncontrolled confounders (calcium, membrane potential, redox status). Partial agreement with reservations.

Both address calibration limitations (C83, C84). OpenEval notes the extrapolation above 42°C is transparently acknowledged as a limitation. Peer reviewers support this acknowledgment and emphasize it as part of broader calibration concerns. Agreement that this is a legitimate methodological constraint.

Both evaluate inhibitor experiments and electron flow pathway inferences (C28, C100, C101). OpenEval finds the pattern internally consistent and biologically plausible. Peer reviewers note strength in coupling measurements with perturbations but criticize 'absence of simultaneous or parallel measurements of other key bioenergetic parameters' limiting cause-effect interpretation. Disagreement on sufficiency of evidence.

Both address MTY localization via subfractionation (C45, C46, C47). OpenEval finds results consistent despite small sample size and considers the inference reasonable. Peer reviewers do not specifically challenge these data but request additional experiments with 'isolated mitochondria and other isolated organelles.' Agreement on data validity but peer reviewers want more evidence.

Both evaluate substrate-dependent temperature modulation and homeostatic regulation (C2, C49-C53, C55). OpenEval finds clear demonstration of homeostatic regulation. Peer reviewers acknowledge evidence supports the notion but critically note 'no outcome measures are reported to document whether the intended objective was achieved' for metabolic interventions. Disagreement on whether homeostasis is demonstrated.

Both address oligomycin experiments (C4, C55). OpenEval finds data supported but mechanistic interpretation speculative. Peer reviewers raise similar concern about lack of validation that intended metabolic effects were achieved. Agreement that mechanistic claims need more support.

Both evaluate AOX rewarming phenomenon (C58-C61, C102, C103). OpenEval finds rewarming well-documented with logical mechanistic inferences. Peer reviewers acknowledge experimental design but emphasize 'absence of simultaneous or parallel measurements of other key bioenergetic parameters limits the ability to interpret potential cause and effect.' Agreement on observation, disagreement on mechanistic interpretation strength.

Both address anisomycin/protein synthesis inhibition experiments (C62, C63, C65-C69). OpenEval finds the surprising result strengthens confidence it's not artifact but notes mechanistic interpretations are speculative. Peer reviewers specifically criticize lack of validation that anisomycin 'decreased ATP demand-OxPhos flux' as intended. Agreement that mechanistic understanding is incomplete.

Both evaluate the central thesis about temperature homeostasis (C6, C7, C72, C146). OpenEval finds the general principle well-supported by collective evidence though mechanistic details need investigation. Peer reviewers find 'physiological relevance remains unclear' and study 'does not substantially clarify the true temperature of mitochondria.' Major disagreement on whether central claims are established.

OpenEval evaluates membrane potential controls (C76-C80) as supported with logical inference that membrane potential effects are negligible. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers elsewhere request better control for membrane potential as a confounder.
OpenEval addresses mito-gTEMP photobleaching limitation (C81, C82) as appropriately acknowledged. No specific peer review evaluation of this limitation found.
